unit.title: Perform advanced welding using gas tungsten arc welding process (GTAW) –Tungsten inert Gas (TIG)

summary: This Level 3 unit takes you beyond basic TIG welding. You will learn to work to a WPS and lead others; to choose and set DC and AC current, balance, frequency and pulse; to choose, size and grind tungsten electrodes; to shield and back purge stainless steel; to choose fillers for stainless steel, aluminium and carbon steel; to weld plate and pipe in all positions while controlling heat; and to inspect, test, finish and record the work safely.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It covers **advanced gas tungsten arc welding (GTAW)**, usually called **TIG** (tungsten inert gas): working to a WPS, current types and polarity, AC balance and frequency, pulse, tungsten electrodes, shielding and back purging, filler metals, positional plate and pipe welding, heat control on stainless steel and aluminium, defects, inspection, heat-tint removal, safety, supervision and records.

TIG gives the most control of any common arc process. It is used where quality and appearance matter most: stainless steel food, beverage and pharmaceutical lines, aluminium boats and fittings, pipe roots, and thin sheet. At Level 3 you are expected to plan TIG work, get it right first time, and coach less experienced welders.
**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust centres and other providers, and welders who lead TIG work on stainless steel, aluminium and pipe.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Work to a WPS and plan the job
Check the WPS against the job, the stock and the welders' qualifications; plan the order of work; stop and report when a condition cannot be met.
Set DC or AC, polarity, balance, frequency, slope, pulse, pre-flow and post-flow; check the torch, cup, gas and cooling.
Choose the type and size for the current and metal; grind safely to the right shape.
Choose the gas and flow; set up dams, tape and vent; purge to the WPS and check it before welding.
Pick the right filler for stainless steel, aluminium, carbon steel and mixed joints, and handle it cleanly.
Weld plate and pipe in all positions
Make roots, fill and cap passes on plate and pipe (including 2G, 5G and 6G pipe), controlling heat and interpass temperature.
Inspect before, during and after; carry out dye penetrant testing; understand radiography; remove heat tint safely.
Control UV, ozone, fume, thorium dust, high-frequency effects and acids; coach and check others; keep records.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on current and polarity, tungstens, torch and gas, back purging, filler metals, preparation, heat control, positions, technique, defects, inspection, safety, equipment, procedures and supervision, with short calculations.

A **written paper**: short answers that need exact terms or figures (for example DCEN, gas lens, 5G, 2G, 4G, purge dam, pickling paste, AC balance, HAZ, a cup size or a cylinder's hours) and essays in full sentences.

**Practical tasks** done as a team: TIG weld stainless steel tube butt joints with an argon back purge, then section and record them; and fabricate an aluminium bracket assembly on AC and check it with dye penetrant.

blocks.note: Many TIG questions are about cause and effect: what happens to the arc, the tungsten and the weld when you change the polarity, balance, frequency, tungsten size or purge. Learn each one as "if I do this, then that happens, because ...".
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Checking a TIG WPS before the job

head: Check
What to look at
rows: Parent metal grade and thickness or pipe size; joint type and preparation; positions
Current type and polarity; current range; travel speed or heat input; pulse settings if used
Tungsten type and size; filler grade and size; shielding gas and flow; back purge gas, flow and oxygen limit
Preheat; maximum interpass temperature; any heat treatment
Inspection and tests required; acceptance standard
Welders qualified to this WPS for the position and size

blocks.p: If a condition cannot be met at the Centre (the right filler grade is not in stock, there is no purge equipment, a welder's test only fuses properly above the WPS current range), **do not change it yourself and carry on.** Stop, tell your supervisor, and wait for an approved answer: the right materials, a revised WPS, or a different WPS that has been qualified. Record what happened. Never write a different figure on the weld record from the one actually used.

flow: Check the WPS, drawings and stock (pipe, fittings, filler, gas, purge equipment, tungstens) before anything is cut
Prepare the ends: cut square, bevel as the WPS says, deburr, clean
Fit up and tack, with purge set up where needed; check gap, root face and alignment
Weld root, fill and cap, checking the purge and interpass temperature
Inspect and test; repair and re-test if needed
Complete the weld records and report
Go through the WPS together: current range, tungsten, filler, gas flow, purge and interpass limits; check their qualification covers the job, or arrange practice and a test first
Demonstrate the set-up and purge, then watch them do it
Have them weld a practice joint on offcuts of the same material, watching torch angle, arc length, filler feeding and how they keep the tungsten clean
Inspect or section the practice joint with them; say what was good and what to improve
On the real job, check their fit-up and purge before they weld, and check the root before the next pass (hold points)
Give feedback calmly, and in private where needed; record their work and report their progress

head: Job
Usual best choice
rows: Root run on thin-wall stainless pipe, with purge
Thin stainless or aluminium work the customer will see
Long fillet welds on a heavy steel trailer
Filling a thick plate butt joint quickly
MMAW or self-shielded flux-cored: the TIG gas shield blows away

head: Current
Heat split
Effect
Used for
rows: About two-thirds of the heat goes into the work, one-third into the tungsten
Deep, narrow fusion; the tungsten stays cool and holds a point
Carbon steel, stainless steel, copper, nickel alloys, titanium: most TIG work
About two-thirds of the heat goes into the tungsten
The tungsten overheats and can melt into the weld unless it is very large; shallow, wide weld; strong cleaning action
Switches between the two many times a second
The electrode-negative (EN) part gives penetration; the electrode-positive (EP) part breaks up the oxide on the surface (cleaning action)

blocks.p: Aluminium is covered by a tough oxide film that melts at about 2 050 °C, while the aluminium under it melts at about 660 °C. The EP part of the AC cycle breaks the oxide up; the EN part puts heat into the plate.

head: Control
Turned one way
Turned the other way
rows: More EN: deeper fusion, narrower bead, cooler tungsten, but less cleaning (a narrower frosted band)
More EP: more cleaning and a wider frosted band, but a hotter tungsten that may ball up and spit, and shallower fusion
Higher: a narrower, more focused arc, easier to direct into a corner or onto thin edges

blocks.p: Many welders start at about 65–75% EN and adjust; follow the WPS and the machine maker. Old transformer sets have no balance control, and their AC follows the mains frequency (50 Hz in Jamaica).

ul: **High-frequency (HF) start:** a high-voltage spark jumps the gap, so the tungsten never touches the work. HF can upset nearby electronics and computer-controlled machines, and can affect heart pacemakers and other implants.
**Lift-arc start:** the tungsten touches the work at very low current and is lifted to start the arc. No HF.
**Scratch start** (on basic DC sets) easily contaminates the tungsten and the weld: avoid it on quality work.
**Upslope and downslope:** the current rises gently at the start and falls gently at the end. Downslope with a little extra filler fills the crater, which stops crater cracks.

**Pre-flow and post-flow:** gas flows before the arc starts and after it stops. Post-flow protects the hot tungsten and the crater while they cool; a common guide is about 1 second for every 10 A (follow the maker). Hold the torch over the crater until the gas stops.

blocks.p: The current switches between a **peak** (for fusion) and a **background** (to let the pool cool a little) at a set pulse frequency. The average current, and so the heat, is lower than the peak: useful on thin stainless steel, to reduce distortion and control the pool in position.

head: Example
Working
Average current
rows: Peak 160 A for 40% of the time; background 40 A for 60%

ul: **Air-cooled torches** suit lower currents (up to roughly 150–200 A, depending on the torch). **Water-cooled torches** are used for higher currents: cooling water keeps the torch head and cable from overheating, so they can be smaller and lighter. Check the coolant level and that the cooler is switched on before welding: a water-cooled torch run dry burns out in seconds.

The **collet** grips the tungsten; the **collet body** holds it and passes the gas. A **gas lens** has fine mesh screens that give a smooth, even (non-turbulent) gas flow, so the tungsten can stick out further for roots deep in a groove or inside corners, with good cover.

**Cups** (nozzles) are usually ceramic. Their size is a number of sixteenths of an inch: a No. 6 cup is 6/16 in, about 9.5 mm across inside; a No. 10 cup about 15.9 mm. A cracked or chipped cup is replaced before welding: it breaks up the gas cover.
Set the gas with a **flowmeter** in litres per minute, to suit the cup (often about 7–15 L/min). Too little lets air in; too much makes the gas turbulent so it draws air in, and wastes gas.

flow: Cables, torch and switch undamaged; connections tight
Cup, collet and collet body (or gas lens) clean and the right size; cup not cracked
Tungsten the right type and size, cleanly ground
Gas: right gas, flowmeter set, hoses and fittings leak-free; purge gas ready
Cooler on and coolant flowing (water-cooled torch)
Return clamp on clean metal; current type, polarity and settings to the WPS
Test on scrap before the job

head: Type
Usual tip colour (check the packet: American and international colours differ)
Notes
rows: Forms a ball on AC; used on old transformer sets; carries less current
Starts well and carries high current on DC, but contains slightly **radioactive** thorium: its grinding dust must not be breathed or swallowed. Being replaced by the types below.
Starts well at low current; AC and DC
Good on AC and DC; a common all-round choice in place of thoriated
Holds a ball and resists contamination on AC transformer sets

blocks.p: Many workshops now use **lanthanated or ceriated** tungstens instead of thoriated, so that grinding does not make radioactive dust.

head: Tungsten diameter
Typical DCEN current (follow the WPS and the maker)

ul: Too thin a tungsten for the current overheats, melts at the tip and can drop into the weld (a tungsten inclusion).
Too thick a tungsten for the current gives a wandering, hard-to-start arc.
On **AC**, the EP half of each cycle heats the tungsten, so for the same current an AC tungsten is usually **larger** than a DC one (or the same size carries much less current).
Grind on a wheel (often diamond) kept **only for tungsten**, so the tungsten is not contaminated with steel grit.
Grind **lengthwise**, so the grinding marks run along the tungsten towards the point. Marks running round it make the arc wander.
A taper about 2 to 2½ times the diameter long is a common starting point.

A **sharper** point (smaller included angle) starts easily and gives a wider arc with less penetration, but wears faster. A **blunter** point (larger included angle) gives a narrower arc, deeper penetration and longer life.
A tiny **flat** on the very end (a truncated point) stops the tip melting off at higher currents.
For AC on an inverter set, a lanthanated or ceriated tungsten ground to a point with a small flat is usual; on old transformer sets, a pure or zirconiated tungsten with a balled end.
Wear safety glasses; use local extraction or a dust-collecting grinder; dispose of the dust as the Centre's rules say.

blocks.p: If the tungsten touches the pool or the filler rod, it picks up metal: the arc wanders, the tip turns grey or black, and bits can drop into the weld. **Stop at once.** Grind out the contaminated spot in the weld, break off the contaminated end of the tungsten, regrind it (or fit a new one), and restart.

With a standard collet body, the tungsten usually sticks out only a few millimetres beyond the cup (often about 3–6 mm). A gas lens allows a longer stick-out (often up to about 10–15 mm) to reach into a groove or corner while keeping good gas cover.

head: Gas
Used for
Notes
rows: Almost all TIG work, and back purging
Heavier than air: it collects in pits and tanks and can push out oxygen
Hotter arc: deeper, wider fusion and faster travel; helium is light, so higher flows are needed
Argon with a little hydrogen (up to about 5%)
Austenitic stainless steel and nickel alloys only
Hotter, cleaner arc with less oxide; **never** on carbon steel or other steels that can harden (hydrogen cracking), or on aluminium (porosity)

blocks.p: When the root of a stainless steel joint is welded, the inside of the root is as hot as the outside. If air reaches it, it oxidises heavily: the root turns dark and crusty ("sugared"), and loses its corrosion resistance. **Back purging** fills the inside of the pipe or the back of the joint with argon, so the root stays clean and bright.

flow: Clean the pipe inside and out with solvent and a stainless-only brush
Fit **purge dams** on each side of the joint (soluble paper dams, inflatable bladders, or discs or bungs)
Tape over the joint gap, and make a small **vent** at the far side so gas can escape and pressure cannot build up
Purge with argon at the WPS flow, passing several times the volume between the dams (the WPS gives the number)
Check the oxygen at the vent with an oxygen meter, where available, until it is below the WPS limit (very low for food and pharmaceutical work)
Turn the purge flow down to a gentle flow for welding
Remove the tape a little at a time as you tack and weld
Keep the purge running for the root **and** the next (hot) pass, because the next pass reheats the root enough for it to oxidise from inside

blocks.note: Too high a purge pressure pushes the molten root inwards, leaving a hollow (concave) root surface: **suck-back**. Purge at the full flow first, then turn it down for welding, and keep the vent open.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Volume of pipe between the dams = π × radius² × length (in mm³; 1 litre = 1 000 000 mm³). Purge time = volume × number of changes ÷ flow.

head: Example
Working
Answer
rows: Inside diameter 60 mm, dams 500 mm apart, 5 volume changes, 4 L/min

blocks.h: Reading the colour of stainless steel welds

head: Colour on and beside the weld
What it means
rows: Some oxidation; the specification says whether it is accepted
Heavier oxide: chromium lost from the surface; usually must be removed on food, water and chemical work
No effective purge: the root is badly oxidised and is usually cut out and rewelded; cleaning cannot restore it

blocks.p: The darker the colour, the thicker the oxide and the more chromium has been taken from the surface, so the steel there can rust or stain.

head: Joint
Usual filler
Why
rows: L = low carbon: less risk of weld decay
Contains molybdenum to match 316's better resistance to salt and chemicals
Extra chromium and nickel allow for dilution by the carbon steel, so the weld stays sound
A filler of the same alloy as 6061 tends to crack as it cools; 4043 resists cracking, 5356 is stronger and matches anodising better
Silicon filler (4043) with high-magnesium alloys forms a brittle compound in the weld
ER70S-2 has extra deoxidisers that suit TIG roots

ul: Keep filler rods clean, dry and labelled, in tubes or their packets. Wear clean gloves: oil and sweat on the rod cause porosity.
Choose a rod diameter that suits the joint and the current.
Keep the hot end of the rod **inside the gas shield** between dabs; never pull it out into the air and then back into the pool, as its oxidised end contaminates the weld.

head: Metal
Preparation
rows: Degrease with solvent; brush with a stainless brush kept only for stainless; use stainless-only grinding discs; keep it off carbon steel benches
Degrease first, then brush with a stainless brush kept only for aluminium; weld soon. Parts cleaned yesterday and left overnight must be cleaned again: new oxide, dust and moisture form.
Grind off mill scale, rust and paint near the joint: TIG is far less tolerant of dirt than MMAW or MIG

ul: **Thick aluminium** conducts heat away so fast that the pool is slow to form: preheat as the WPS allows (some heat-treated alloys lose strength if overheated, so keep to its limit).

Check fit-up before welding: gap, root face, and **misalignment (hi-lo)** between pipe ends with a hi-lo gauge, against the WPS limit. A step at the root gives lack of fusion on the high side. If it is outside the limit, break the tacks and refit.
Tacks are well fused and ground or feathered at each end, so the root can blend into them.

head: Code
Plate or pipe position
rows: Plate groove welds: flat / horizontal / vertical / overhead
Fillet welds: flat / horizontal / vertical / overhead
Axis horizontal, pipe **rolled** so the weld is made on top
Axis **vertical**: the weld runs round level (horizontal)
Axis horizontal and **fixed**: welded from the bottom up each side (flat, vertical and overhead)
Axis fixed at **45°**: the most demanding position, often used for all-position tests

ul: Arc length about the diameter of the tungsten; keep it short and steady.
Torch tilted about 10–20° in the direction of travel; filler rod at a low angle (about 15–20°) to the work, fed into the leading edge of the pool.
Watch the pool, not the arc: add filler when the pool has formed and wetted both edges.
In an open-root pass, a small **keyhole** at the front of the pool shows that the root is penetrating fully. Keep it the same size: growing means too much heat; closing means too little.

**Walking the cup:** the cup is rested on the groove faces and rocked from side to side to move the torch along. It gives a very steady arc length and even ripples, and is common on pipe with a larger cup and a gas lens. **Freehand** welding holds the cup clear of the work.
Feather the tacks and fuse into them; finish each stop with downslope, fill the crater, and hold the torch over it for the post-flow.
Some pipe roots use a **consumable insert** (a ring of filler fitted in the joint), which the root pass melts in.

blocks.p: The WPS for stainless steel often sets a **maximum interpass temperature** (often about 150 °C; follow the WPS), to limit grain growth, distortion and weld decay. Check it with a contact thermometer or a temperature-indicating crayon before each pass, never by touch. Let the joint cool in air unless the WPS says otherwise.

blocks.h: Heat control on thin stainless steel

head: Problem
Why
Control
rows: Stainless steel expands about half as much again as carbon steel and conducts heat only about a third as well, so heat stays in one place
Close, even tacks; short runs in a balanced or skip order; clamping; copper chill bars
Held at about 450–850 °C too long, chromium joins with carbon beside the weld, and that zone can rust later
L-grade filler and base metal; low current; interpass limit
Good gas cover front and back; trailing shields on long welds; clean off afterwards

ul: **Copper chill bars** clamped behind or beside the joint draw heat away and support the root.
**Pulsed TIG** lowers the average heat while keeping fusion.
Use the lowest current that gives full fusion.
AC with balance and frequency set; argon (or argon-helium for thick sections).
Wait for the pool to form and go shiny, then add filler quickly and travel faster than on steel.
Use downslope and add filler at the end to fill the crater: aluminium cracks easily in an unfilled crater.
Aluminium does not glow or change colour when hot: treat every part as hot and mark it.

head: Calculation
Method
Worked example
rows: 7 000 L ÷ 8 L/min = 875 min, about 14½ hours of arc time
No. 6: about 9.5 mm; No. 10: about 15.9 mm

head: Defect
Common TIG causes
Prevention
rows: Tungsten inclusions (show as bright white spots on a radiograph)
Tungsten dipped in the pool or touched by the rod
Current too high for the tungsten size
Right size and polarity; HF or lift-arc start; stop, grind out and regrind after any touch
Dirty base metal or filler; oily gloves
Gas flow too low or too high; leaks; draughts
Clean, dry materials; correct flow; screens; leak checks
Purge properly and check it before welding
Too much heat at the root
Gentle purge during welding; control heat
Current too low; travel too fast
Gap too small, root face too big, hi-lo
Correct settings, fit-up and torch position
Current too high or arc too long
Too little filler at the edges
Shorter arc; add filler at the toes
Arc stopped suddenly, especially on aluminium
Downslope and add filler to fill the crater
Regrind lengthwise; move the clamp; screens

head: Stage
Checks
rows: Material grade, WPS, welder qualification; fit-up, root gap, hi-lo alignment; cleanliness; purge set-up
Purge oxygen, current, interpass temperature; each pass inspected
Outside: cap size and shape, undercut, porosity, cracks, heat tint. Inside the root: penetration, suck-back and colour (mirror, torch or borescope). Then NDT and pressure tests as specified.

blocks.p: PT finds fine cracks and pores that break the surface, on any non-porous metal. It is used on stainless steel and aluminium because magnetic particle testing does not work on non-magnetic metals.

flow: **Clean** the surface with the kit's cleaner and let it dry
Apply the **penetrant** (usually red) and leave it for the dwell time on the product sheet
**Remove the excess**: wipe with a dry cloth, then with a cloth just dampened with cleaner; never spray cleaner straight onto the area, or it washes the penetrant out of the cracks
Apply a thin, even coat of **developer** (white)
**Inspect** in good light after the development time: red lines or dots on the white show flaws
Record the results with a sketch or photo, then clean off

ul: **Radiography (RT)** uses X-rays or gamma rays to show flaws inside the weld: porosity (dark round spots), lack of fusion, cracks, and tungsten inclusions (bright white spots, because tungsten is very dense). It is common on process pipework and is done by qualified radiographers behind barriers.
**Ultrasonic testing (UT)** finds internal flaws in thicker sections.
Finished pipe spools may be **pressure tested**.
Records: joint number, welder, WPS, filler batch, purge details, inspection and test results, repairs and retests, signed and dated.

head: Method
Points to know
rows: Stainless brush (stainless-only), fine abrasive or polishing
Simple; for light tint; must not leave iron or a rough surface

Strong acids (often nitric and hydrofluoric). Read the SDS; acid-resistant gloves, face shield, long sleeves and apron; ventilation; leave on only for the maker's time; rinse as the SDS says; collect the rinse water and waste for proper disposal, never into a drain or the sea
A low-voltage unit with a mild electrolyte cleans the tint; safer than pickling paste
A treatment after cleaning that helps the protective chromium oxide film re-form

blocks.note: Hydrofluoric acid burns may not hurt at first, yet they can do deep damage hours later. Any skin contact with pickling paste is treated at once: wash with plenty of water and follow the SDS first aid (many workplaces keep calcium gluconate gel for this), and get medical help.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Salt air on the coast attacks stainless steel. Grade 316 (with molybdenum) resists salt and chloride pitting much better than 304, so it is the usual choice for seaside handrails and boat fittings. Keep all carbon steel grinding sparks and tools away from stainless work: iron specks rust within days in the sea air.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Health and safety for advanced TIG

head: Hazard
Why it matters
Controls
rows: TIG gives very strong UV, especially on aluminium and at high current; it burns eyes and skin quickly, even from reflections
Correct filter shade for the current (often about 10–13)
UV from the arc turns oxygen into ozone, which irritates the lungs; worst with aluminium
TIG makes little smoke, but stainless fume contains harmful chromium and nickel compounds
Local extraction close to the arc
Grinding thoriated tungsten makes slightly radioactive dust that is harmful if breathed or swallowed
Use lanthanated or ceriated tungstens instead
Otherwise a dedicated grinder with dust collection, and safe disposal
Upsets nearby electronics and computer-controlled machines; can affect pacemakers and other implants
Keep HF sets and cables away from electronics, or use lift-arc
Anyone with an implant gets medical advice before working near welding
Higher risk on AC and in wet or hot, sweaty conditions
Heavier than air; collects low and displaces oxygen without warning
Confined spaces: permit, gas testing, ventilation
Pickling paste burns; solvent vapour can catch fire, and chlorinated solvents near the arc can form a poisonous gas
SDS, PPE and ventilation for acids
Solvents used away from the arc and stored closed
Aluminium and stainless steel give no colour warning when hot
Treat all welded parts as hot; use tongs and mark them

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise with your instructor.

ul: I can check a TIG WPS against the job and say what to do if a condition cannot be met.
I can plan TIG work in the right order and coach a less experienced welder.
I can explain DCEN, DCEP and AC, and why aluminium is welded on AC.
I can set AC balance and frequency and explain their effects.
I can explain HF and lift-arc starting, slope, pre-flow, post-flow and pulse, and work out a pulsed average current.
I can choose a tungsten type and size, and grind it safely to the right shape.
I can deal correctly with a contaminated tungsten.
I can choose a shielding gas, set the flow and pick the right cup or gas lens.
I can set up and check a back purge and work out the purge time.
I can read the colour of a stainless steel weld and say what it means.
I can choose fillers for stainless steel, aluminium, carbon steel and stainless-to-carbon-steel joints.
I can prepare and fit up stainless steel, aluminium and carbon steel for TIG, including checking hi-lo.
I can name the plate and pipe positions, and weld an open root with a steady keyhole.
I can control heat, distortion and interpass temperature on thin stainless steel.
I can name TIG defects, their causes and prevention, and carry out dye penetrant testing in the right order.
I can remove heat tint safely and control the health hazards of advanced TIG work.

terms: AC balance
The control that sets the share of time an AC arc spends electrode-negative and electrode-positive
Back purging
Filling the back of a joint or the inside of a pipe with argon so the root does not oxidise
Chill bar
A copper bar clamped near a joint to draw heat away and support the root
DCEN
Direct current, electrode negative: the usual TIG polarity for steels
Downslope
A gentle fall in current at the end of a weld, to fill the crater
Gas lens
A torch fitting with fine mesh screens that gives a smooth, even gas flow
HAZ (heat-affected zone)
The parent metal beside a weld that was changed by the heat but did not melt
Heat tint
Coloured oxide on and beside a stainless steel weld, from straw to grey
HF start
Starting the arc with a high-frequency spark, so the tungsten does not touch the work
Hi-lo
Misalignment between the inside surfaces of two pipe ends or plates at the root
Interpass temperature
The temperature of the joint just before the next pass
Keyhole
A small hole at the front of the pool showing full root penetration
L grade
A low-carbon stainless steel or filler (for example 308L), which reduces weld decay
Lanthanated tungsten
A tungsten containing lanthanum oxide; a common replacement for thoriated
Pickling paste
An acid paste used to remove heat tint from stainless steel
Post-flow
Gas that keeps flowing after the arc stops, to protect the tungsten and crater
Purge dam
A plug or disc fitted inside a pipe on each side of the joint to hold the purge gas in
RT
Radiographic testing: X-ray or gamma-ray examination of the inside of a weld
Suck-back
A hollow (concave) root surface, often from too much purge pressure
Tungsten inclusion
A piece of tungsten trapped in the weld; bright white on a radiograph
Walking the cup
Rocking the cup on the groove faces to move the torch along a joint
Weld decay
Loss of corrosion resistance beside a stainless steel weld held too long at 450–850 °C
1G, 2G, 5G, 6G (pipe)
Pipe rolled / axis vertical / axis horizontal and fixed / axis at 45° and fixed

c1.title: Stainless pipe spools in Spanish Town
c1.text: Sheneil leads a small team TIG welding 316L stainless steel pipe spools for a beverage plant in Spanish Town, St Catherine. The pipe has an inside diameter of 100 mm, and the purge dams are fitted 800 mm apart. The WPS calls for an argon purge at 8 L/min, passing at least 5 times the volume between the dams before the arc is struck. One carbon steel support bracket must also be welded directly to a stainless spool. On one finished joint, the inside of the root is grey, rough and crusty.

c2.title: An aluminium boat in Discovery Bay
c2.text: Rohan is TIG welding a small aluminium boat at a boatyard in Discovery Bay, St Ann, with an inverter AC set. The hull plates are 5083 alloy and the frames are 6061. His welds show a very wide, frosted cleaning band, and the balled end of his tungsten keeps spitting small bits into the pool.

c3.title: Preparing for a 6G test in Lucea
c3.text: Tamoy is preparing for a 6G pipe test at a training centre in Lucea, Hanover: carbon steel pipe with an open root, TIG welded with ER70S-2 filler. During a practice root, his tungsten dips into the pool. On another practice joint, the two pipe ends are 2 mm out of line at one point after tacking, and the WPS allows 1 mm. His post-flow is set to 2 seconds at 120 A, and his tungsten tip comes out blue-black after each stop.

c4.title: Supervising the TIG bay in Black River
c4.text: Everton supervises the TIG bay at a fabrication shop in Black River, St Elizabeth. On his first day, a new trainee tells him that he has a heart pacemaker. The bay's only bench grinder is used both for sharpening 2% thoriated tungstens and for dressing mild steel chisels. One welder has set his argon flowmeter to 30 L/min on a No. 6 cup, saying that more gas gives better cover.

c5.title: Beachfront handrails in Negril
c5.text: Dujon's team is TIG welding stainless steel handrails for a hotel on the beach in Negril, Westmoreland. The client's specification asks for all heat tint to be removed, and the team plans to use a pickling paste whose safety data sheet (SDS) says it contains nitric and hydrofluoric acids. A week after the first rails are fitted, brown rust spots appear on them near where another contractor has been grinding mild steel railings.

questions.q: About how long must the pipe be purged before Sheneil's team strikes the arc?
o: About 1 minute
About 4 minutes
About 20 minutes
About 40 minutes
questions.why: Volume = π × 50² × 800 ≈ 6 283 000 mm³ ≈ 6.3 litres. Five volumes ≈ 31.4 litres, and 31.4 ÷ 8 L/min ≈ 3.9 minutes, so about 4 minutes, then check the oxygen at the vent if a meter is available.

questions.q: Which filler should be used to weld the carbon steel bracket to the stainless spool?
o: ER316L, to match the spool
ER308L
ER70S-2, to match the bracket
ER309L
questions.why: ER309L has extra chromium and nickel, so the weld stays sound when it mixes with the carbon steel. A filler matched to either metal alone can give a crack-prone or rust-prone weld.

questions.q: What should be done about the joint whose root is grey, rough and crusty inside?
o: Pickle the inside of the root until it is bright again
Wire-brush the inside of the root with a stainless brush
Cut it out and reweld it with a proper purge
Accept it, as the outside of the weld looks good
questions.why: A sugared root is heavily oxidised and has lost its corrosion resistance; cleaning cannot restore the metal underneath. The joint is cut out and rewelded, after finding out why the purge failed.

questions.q: Why should the purge be kept running while the second (hot) pass is welded?
o: The second pass reheats the root, which could oxidise inside
Argon cools the pipe so that the second pass does not distort it
The WPS only allows the gas flow to be changed between joints
Turning the purge off would let the dams fall out of the pipe
questions.why: The hot pass heats the root high enough to oxidise again from the inside. The purge stays on until the root has been protected through that pass.

questions.q: What should Rohan change to cure the wide frosted band and the spitting tungsten?
o: Increase the electrode-positive time on the balance
Raise the current so the pool forms more quickly
Lower the AC frequency to give a softer, wider arc
More EN on the balance, or a larger tungsten
questions.why: Too much electrode-positive time over-cleans and overheats the tungsten, so it balls and spits. More EN time (or a larger tungsten) cools the tungsten and narrows the cleaning band.

questions.q: Which filler should Rohan use on the 5083 hull plates?
o: ER4043, as it resists hot cracking best of all
ER1100 pure aluminium, for softness
ER5356 (or ER5183), a magnesium filler
ER308L, as boats need to resist rust
questions.why: With high-magnesium alloys such as 5083, a silicon filler like 4043 forms a brittle compound in the weld. Magnesium fillers such as 5356 or 5183 give a strong, tough weld for marine work.

questions.q: Which tungsten and tip shape suit his inverter AC set best?
o: Lanthanated, pointed with a small flat
Pure tungsten with a large ball on the end
Thoriated, ground to a needle-sharp point
Any type, as long as it is the thinnest one
questions.why: Inverter AC sets work well with lanthanated or ceriated tungstens ground to a point with a small flat. Large balled pure tungstens belong to old transformer sets, and too thin a tungsten overheats on AC.

questions.q: What should Tamoy do when his tungsten dips into the pool?
o: Raise the current to burn off the metal on the tungsten
Carry on, as the next pass will melt in any tungsten
Stop, grind out the spot, and regrind the tungsten
Wipe the tungsten tip on a clean cloth and carry on
questions.why: A contaminated tungsten makes the arc wander and can leave tungsten inclusions, which show as bright white spots on a radiograph. Stop, grind the contaminated spot out of the weld, break off and regrind the tungsten, then restart.

questions.q: What should be done about the joint that is 2 mm out of line after tacking?
o: Weld it, adding extra filler on the high side of the root
Weld it, and grind the root flush from inside afterwards
Weld it with a hotter root pass to melt out the step
Break the tacks and refit it within the 1 mm allowed
questions.why: Hi-lo outside the WPS limit leaves a step at the root, which gives lack of fusion on the high side. The fit-up is corrected before welding, not covered up during it.

questions.q: What do the blue-black tungsten tips tell Tamoy about his post-flow?
o: It is too long, and the gas is cooling the tungsten too fast
Too short: lengthen it, holding the torch over the crater
It does not matter, as post-flow only protects the crater
It is right, as tungsten always turns blue when it cools
questions.why: The tungsten oxidises when the gas stops before it has cooled. A common guide is about 1 second per 10 A, so about 12 seconds at 120 A, with the torch held over the crater until the gas stops.

questions.q: Tamoy wants deeper root fusion and longer tungsten life at the same current. How should he grind the tungsten?
o: With a blunter point, a larger included angle
To a needle-sharp point, as sharp as he can get
With a balled end, as for AC aluminium work
With grinding marks running round the tungsten
questions.why: A blunter point gives a narrower, more focused arc with deeper penetration and wears more slowly. A very sharp point gives a wider arc and burns away faster; marks running round the tungsten make the arc wander.

questions.q: What should Everton do about the trainee with a pacemaker?
o: Ask him to get medical advice before he works near welding
Let him weld, as long as the set uses lift-arc starting only
Let him weld with the torch cable kept over one shoulder
Give him a darker filter shade and let him start welding
questions.why: HF starting and the magnetic fields round welding cables can affect pacemakers. He should not work near welding until his doctor has advised what is safe; lift-arc alone does not settle it.

questions.q: What is wrong with how the bay sharpens its thoriated tungstens?
o: Nothing, as tungsten dust is no different from ordinary steel dust
Only the grinder's wheel needs changing after each use
Thoriated tungsten should only ever be sharpened with a hand file
Radioactive dust is spread, and steel grit gets on the tungsten
questions.why: Thoriated grinding dust is slightly radioactive and must not be spread round a shared grinder, and steel grit on the wheel contaminates the tungsten. Use a dedicated grinder with dust collection, or change to lanthanated tungstens.

questions.q: What is the problem with setting 30 L/min on a No. 6 cup?
o: The turbulent gas pulls air in, causing porosity
The cylinder pressure will soon fall too low to weld
The arc will be too cold to melt the stainless
The cup will overheat and crack in a short time
questions.why: Too much gas through a small cup leaves it as a turbulent jet that drags air into the shield, causing porosity, and wastes argon. Set the flow the WPS gives for the cup size.

questions.q: Some pickling paste gets on a worker's wrist, but it does not hurt. What should happen?
o: Nothing, as there is no pain and so no harm done
Wipe it off and carry on, then check it at lunch
Wash at once, follow the SDS first aid, get help
Cover it with a plaster to keep the acid off his clothes
questions.why: Hydrofluoric acid burns may not hurt at first but can do deep damage later. Wash with plenty of water straight away, follow the SDS first aid (often calcium gluconate gel), and get medical help.

questions.q: What most likely caused the brown rust spots on the new stainless rails?
o: The rails were not welded with an L-grade filler rod
Iron from the nearby steel grinding landed on them
The pickling paste was left on for too short a time
The sea air always makes stainless steel rust
questions.why: Hot sparks from grinding carbon steel embed iron in the stainless surface, and the iron rusts in the salt air. The rails are cleaned and passivated, and carbon steel work is kept well away from stainless work.

questions.q: Why is grade 316 usually chosen over 304 for these beachfront handrails?
o: It is softer and easier to bend into shape on site
Its molybdenum resists salt pitting better
It can be welded without any shielding gas
It never shows heat tint after welding
questions.why: 316 contains molybdenum, which gives much better resistance to chloride (salt) pitting than 304. That matters on a Jamaican beachfront, where salt spray is constant.

questions.q: In dye penetrant testing, why is the excess penetrant removed with a cloth just dampened with cleaner, not by spraying cleaner on the weld?
o: Spraying wastes cleaner, which is costly
Spraying can wash penetrant out of the cracks
Spraying leaves a film the developer cannot cover
Spraying makes the penetrant dry too quickly
questions.why: A direct spray of cleaner can rinse the penetrant out of fine cracks, so they would not show under the developer. Wiping removes only the surface excess.

questions.q: A gas supplier offers an argon-hydrogen mix for faster TIG welding. Where can it be used?
o: On any steel, as long as the welds are kept cool
On aluminium, to break up its oxide more quickly
On carbon steel pipe roots, for deeper penetration
On austenitic stainless steel, if the WPS allows
questions.why: A little hydrogen gives a hotter, cleaner arc on austenitic stainless steel and some nickel alloys. On carbon and other hardenable steels it causes hydrogen cracking, and on aluminium it causes porosity.

questions.q: A pulsed TIG set gives a peak of 150 A for half the time and a background of 50 A for the other half. What is the average current?
questions.why: Average = (150 × 0.5) + (50 × 0.5) = 75 + 25 = 100 A. The weld gets the fusion of the 150 A peaks with the heat of about 100 A, so there is less distortion.
